reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked CDKL5 gene, with most affected patients being female because of the greater severity in males
Seizures usually begin in the first few months of life, frequently as early tonic or clonic seizures and epileptic spasms
A distinctive hypermotor-tonic-spasms sequence within a single seizure has been described
Development is severely impaired with profound intellectual disability, absent speech, hand stereotypies and cortical visual impairment
There is clinical overlap with Rett syndrome, but classic MECP2-related regression is not the typical pattern
Seizures are usually drug-resistant despite an early honeymoon period in some children
Comprehensive genetic testing establishes the diagnosis and distinguishes it from related encephalopathies
reference.pathophysiology: CDKL5 deficiency disorder results from loss-of-function variants in the X-linked CDKL5 gene, which encodes a serine-threonine kinase important for neuronal maturation, dendritic and synaptic development, and regulation of excitatory and inhibitory signalling. Deficient kinase activity disrupts synaptic function and network connectivity in the developing brain, producing early-onset refractory seizures and a severe developmental encephalopathy. X-linkage and patterns of X-inactivation account for the marked female predominance and phenotypic variability.
additionalDifferentials: West syndrome (infantile spasms) of other cause
Other early-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Targeted CDKL5 testing or an epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing
EEG, which may be normal early and later shows multifocal or high-amplitude epileptiform abnormalities
Brain MRI, usually normal early, to exclude structural causes
Ophthalmological and visual assessment for cortical visual impairment
redFlags: Refractory early-infantile seizures including epileptic spasms
Feeding difficulties, recurrent aspiration or respiratory compromise
Emergence of the characteristic hypermotor-tonic-spasms seizure sequence
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have lifelong drug-resistant epilepsy and severe intellectual and motor disability with limited independent function. Life expectancy can be reduced by complications including respiratory illness and SUDEP, though many survive into adulthood with supportive care.
pitfalls: Assuming Rett syndrome without genetic confirmation despite overlapping features
Interpreting an early normal EEG or MRI as excluding the disorder
Missing cortical visual impairment and its impact on development
Persisting with escalating polytherapy without acknowledging drug resistance
management: Antiseizure medication for the drug-resistant epilepsy, using agents such as sodium valproate, vigabatrin or corticosteroids for spasms, and newer options such as ganaxolone or cannabidiol
Ketogenic diet as an adjunct for refractory seizures
Vagus nerve stimulation or epilepsy surgery in selected refractory cases
Multidisciplinary developmental support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and communication therapy
Vision support and low-vision aids for cortical visual impairment
Management of comorbidities including feeding difficulties (with gastrostomy where needed), gastro-oesophageal reflux, scoliosis, and sleep and gastrointestinal problems
Awareness of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy with a seizure emergency and rescue-medication plan
Genetic counselling regarding the X-linked CDKL5 variant and recurrence risk
